title: 'Alpha-gal follows none of the rules': Why a red-meat allergy triggered by tick bites is perplexing scientists
summary: When alpha-gal syndrome first emerged, it was a baffling medical mystery. Today, diagnoses are rising, yet much about this potentially life-threatening condition remains unexplained.
body: Sandra Tiguila, an adventurous eater, enjoyed a bison sausage breakfast sandwich while dining out in August of 2025. On the drive home, she noticed a rash appearing on her wrist. The burning sensation spread to her arms and legs, making it nearly impossible to sleep. In the days to come, she tried creams, pills, injections; nothing helped. Ten days later, Tiguila ate out again, ordering a steak. When her face swelled up, her boyfriend drove her to the emergency room. A doctor tested her for diseases carried by ticks. Tiguila, who lives in Carbondale, Illinois, had been bitten twice that June. Tiguila went home and the next morning, as she was drinking coffee with her usual supplement of bovine collagen for joint, hair and nail health, the test results came in. She had developed a red meat allergy that’s activated by tick bites. "I immediately dumped that coffee down the sink," says Tiguila. She started avoiding all mammal products — the main way to manage this rising and occasionally life-threatening allergy. Known as alpha-gal syndrome, the condition arises when the immune system reacts to a certain sugar molecule, called alpha-gal, that’s found in red meat. Symptoms range from a…

body: Avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager. Since then, he’s cycled through a few prosthetics. But his latest is different—it’s wired up to nerves in the upper part of his forearm and allows him to feel pressure. For the first time in years, he can use his left limb to handle delicate objects like grapes, eggs, and a loved one’s hand. Davidson, who is taking part in a clinical trial run by the University of Utah, is the ninth person to have this experimental device implanted in his arm. But he’s the first to take it home and use it independently. The hand is part of the bionic LUKE arm, named after Luke Skywalker of Star Wars , who was fitted with a lifelike prosthetic arm after his own was light-sabered off . The arm was developed in the 2000s , initially trialed in 2014 , and approved by the FDA that same year. The trial that Davidson is enrolled in isn’t so focused on the arm itself but on a new way to connect it to a person’s nervous system. The connection allows users to control movements and receive feedback about how much pressure they’re applying. title: 'Like designing a new key to open a defective lock': AI-designed protein tricks defective insulin receptors into working
summary: Scientists reported that an AI-designed protein can activate broken insulin receptors in lab mice, hinting at a potential new treatment for some forms of severe insulin resistance.
body: A protein designed with the help of artificial intelligence (AI) has successfully switched on faulty insulin receptors in lab mice even when insulin itself couldn't. The findings hint at a new way to treat certain rare, life-threatening genetic disorders that cause insulin resistance , in which the body's cells don't respond well to the blood-sugar-controlling hormone. In a study published Wednesday (Nov. 25) in the journal Science Translational Medicine , researchers found that the AI-designed protein, called RF-409, lowered blood sugar and reduced damage to the pancreas in mice with a genetic form of severe insulin resistance. This, in turn, prevented dangerous weight loss that typically comes with the condition. When blood sugar rises, the pancreas releases insulin, a hormone that binds to proteins called insulin receptors on the surface of cells. This changes the receptors' shape, triggering a series of chemical signals that ultimately help bring blood sugar levels back down. But mutations in the gene that encodes the insulin receptor can disrupt this process. More than 150 such mutations have been linked to inherited forms of insulin resistance . title: 'A new record in quantum error correction': Scientists say breakthrough brings powerful, fault-tolerant quantum computers closer to reality
summary: Quantinuum's Helios processor achieved a record-low failure rate of just 0.0005%, suggesting fault-tolerant quantum systems may need far fewer qubits than previously thought.
body: Scientists at Quantinuum say they've set a new record in quantum error correction that brings large-scale, fault-tolerant systems one step closer. The team claims their 98-qubit quantum system, Helios , demonstrated a failure rate of just 0.0005% in tests of its quantum memory, which is equivalent to an estimated five uncorrectable errors per million rounds of error checking. This rate bests the previous benchmark set by Google's 105-qubit Willow quantum chip , which demonstrated an estimated 772 uncorrectable errors per million rounds in comparable tests , for an error rate of 0.0772%. The result brings quantum computing closer to the "megaquop regime," where systems can run over a million operations without encountering an error, the researchers said. They detailed their findings in a study uploaded Oct. 16 to the arXiv preprint server. In a statement , Robin Blume-Kohout , co-director of Sandia National Laboratories' Quantum Performance Lab, called the achievement "a significant milestone that quantum computing researchers have been working toward for many years." title: 2,900-year-old sanctuary discovered on Greek mountaintop may have been a destination for Artemis worship
summary: Archaeologists have found the remains of a 2,900-year-old sanctuary on an island mountaintop, where ancient Greeks may have worshipped the goddess Artemis.
body: The discovery of a 2,900-year-old mountaintop sanctuary on a Mediterranean island shows the ancient Greek veneration for high mountains and their link to the Greek gods, archaeologists say. The sanctuary was found during new excavations on Euboea, a very large island only about 30 miles (50 kilometers) northeast of Athens. The sanctuary did not include any buildings, such as a temple. Archaeologists think it was used for offerings and feasting by worshippers for hundreds of years, from about the ninth century B.C. until the first or second century A.D., during Imperial Roman times. "We know that in the ancient Greek world, religious life was not limited to large temples and urban sanctuaries," excavation leader Chloé Chezeaux , an archaeologist at the Swiss School of Archeology in Greece, told Live Science in an email. "There were also many places of worship in the countryside and in the mountains." "An exceptional concentration of pottery" Chezeaux led the excavations this year near the summit of Elatias, one of the highest peaks of Mount Olympus on Euboea. Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing. Given “the way we approach model sentience and moral status,” Anthropic wrote—which is to say it takes the possibility more seriously than any other AI company—it might adopt more rules and restrictions than its competitors to make sure its AI models are treated well.  Anthropic counts a number of respected philosophers in its camp, and the company’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it important they are protected from harm.  This thinking isn’t all that fringe. title: Why using rocks for carbon removal could eventually reduce crop growth
summary: Tech companies are investing a lot of hope and money in rocks. Google, Microsoft, and others have committed hundreds of millions of dollars to get startups to spread crushed basalt, olivine, or other alkaline materials across farms, in an effort to capture carbon from the air and lock it away. A nu…
body: Tech companies are investing a lot of hope and money in rocks. Google, Microsoft, and others have committed hundreds of millions of dollars to get startups to spread crushed basalt, olivine, or other alkaline materials across farms, in an effort to capture carbon from the air and lock it away. A number of influential models have found that this approach, known as enhanced rock weathering (ERW), could eventually remove 3 billion to 8 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide per year, helping to slow or one day even reverse global warming. An additional promise is that these applications of rock could help farmers by improving the quality of their soil. But a pair of preprint studies set for release today raise serious questions about how much material could be added to that soil before it may actually reduce the crop yields that are essential to farmers’ livelihoods, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report.  Cutting back on the rock applications to prevent these negative effects would shrink the method’s carbon dioxide removal capacity, likely capping it at less than a billion tons per year. title: 'A future where EVs charge simply by parking': New positioning system could make wireless EV charging much more efficient
summary: A new positioning technology could make autonomous vehicles and robotaxis more reliable at recharging themselves.
body: (Image credit: 2026 Ryotaro Hada et al. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. ) Researchers in Japan have developed a new technology that could enable electric vehicles (EVs) to charge "simply by parking". Wireless charging is still relatively nascent in the EV market, but scientists hope that integrating more wireless charging devices into roads and parking spaces will move the EV industry away from bulky plug-in infrastructure. It uses the same wireless power transfer technology found in modern smartphones and consumer electronics: a transmitter coil inside in a ground pad generates an oscillating magnetic field , which induces an electric current in a receiver coil underneath the vehicle. This current recharges the EV's battery cells. However, small misalignments between the two coils can affect how quickly and efficiently the battery recharges. This new system uses short-range radio signals to determine the position of the vehicle's magnetic charging coil relative to the charging device in the ground, including its distance and angle. This helps the EV and its driver get into the optimal position for efficient charging. The technology could be particularly useful for driverless "robotaxis…

title: Brains of people with PTSD have unique epigenetic marks, study finds
summary: The brains of people with PTSD bear molecular changes that differ from those in people with other conditions, like depression, a new study finds.
body: A study of hundreds of brains has revealed molecular differences in people with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) that are not found in individuals without the condition. These molecular marks also differ from those seen in the brains of people with other conditions, like depression, the research found. Our environment and experiences influence how our genes work, affecting which genes can be turned on. Rather than changing genes' underlying code, the environment can trigger what are known as epigenetic changes , which include certain chemicals that attach to DNA molecules and change their structure. One such epigenetic change, called methylation, can work like a "dimmer switch" for genes, or even completely block certain genes from turning on. "These epigenetic features of the brain are important for shaping the way the brain functions," study co-author Frances Champagne , a psychologist at the University of Texas at Austin, told Live Science. "This can give us some insight into why individuals with PTSD develop PTSD, or how [their brains] are different from a healthy brain." title: An Anthropic mathematician claims to have proven the Riemann hypothesis. We have to rethink how we reward expertise.
summary: AI has upended the math community with a flood of results. We have to rethink how we assess which questions and answers matter — putting humans back at the center.
body: An Anthropic mathematician using Claude claims to have proven the most famous problem in math — the Riemann hypothesis — in the latest, but potentially most consequential, example of artificial intelligence (AI) producing stunning math results. AI has steamrolled its way into the math community. Anthropic's proof will certainly and rightly be scrutinized, but rather than picking apart every single result these models produce, we should respond by changing how we evaluate and reward expertise — placing less weight on the volume of results and more on the human judgment required to decide which questions and answers matter. Without this shift, we risk drowning genuine insight in a flood of plausible but poorly understood mathematics. title: Quantum entanglement could thwart hackers and scammers, physicists reveal
summary: In a first-of-its-kind experiment, physicists used pairs of entangled photons to verify a person's location. That's a step toward anchoring digital security to the physical world.
body: For the first time, physicists have used quantum entanglement to verify a person's physical location. That could one day make it much harder for hackers to pretend to be somewhere they're not, the team says. In the new study, published Wednesday (Nov. 18) in the journal Nature , researchers at the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) used pairs of entangled photons (particles of light) to confirm that a participant was at a specific spot between two stations on NIST's campus in Boulder, Colorado. The method is called quantum position verification, and this is the first complete demonstration of it. If the technology matures, it could help protect health records, stop remote attackers from sending commands to power grids or water treatment plants, block unauthorized stock trades and thwart phishing attacks carried out over phone or video calls, according to a statement . "It's a totally new application for quantum networks," Shalm said. "You can add another layer of security to these systems that anchors a lot of this digital security to a position." title: 'I would want to know my horse's backstory': Live Science readers share which animals they'd want to speak with
summary: Recently, Live Science asked its readers which animal they'd want to communicate with, based on a new study that leveraged AI to decode different vocalizations of zebra finches.
body: Recently, University of California, Berkeley ethologist Julie Elie used artificial intelligence (AI) and behavioral experiments to decode the different vocalizations of zebra finches ( Taeniopygia guttata ), bringing scientists one step closer to talking to animals . Birds are just some of many animals that experts hope to understand and communicate with. Scientists are also deciphering the clicks and calls of sperm whales and humpback whales . Some animals, like cats, can change their meows depending on what they're seeking from their owners, such as food or attention. In the wake of Elie's new findings, Live Science asked its readers what animal they would want to talk to if they could. Over 550 people voted in our poll, with 54% picking dog. The next-largest voting group, 28% of respondents, chose cat. The comments reflected the obvious trend of readers wanting to speak to their pets. One commenter wrote, "Cats, simply because I've had more of them as pets over the decades than anything else. title: New study rewrites the role of a major speech hub in the brain
summary: Wernicke's area was thought to be mostly linked to understanding speech. A landmark new study has something more to say.
body: A new study has rewritten the role of one of the brain's major speech hubs, opening new possibilities for treating people who can't communicate verbally due to brain damage. The study, published Thursday (Nov. 19) in the journal Science , may help to solve a 150-year-old mystery in neuroscience. Nowadays, neuroscientists use cutting-edge tools to tease apart the junctions and wiring of our complex brains. But some basic theories in the field are far from new and rest on past discoveries. One of those theories concerns how the brain produces and comprehends speech. In the 1860s, German neuroanatomist Carl Wernicke identified an area of the brain that is critical to speech and usually found in the temporal lobe on the left side of the organ. Damage to Wernicke's area makes it challenging for people to understand what others are saying ‪—‬ a condition known as Wernicke's aphasia . Therefore, the brain region has been primarily thought of as a decoder that helps us break down the meaning of other people's speech. Wernicke's area (red) is found in the left temporal lobe. title: The immune system 'remembers' germs by tweaking its epigenetics, study shows
summary: A new study helps explain how the immune system's first line of defense stays ready to fight off germs and diseases.
body: The immune system has several ways of remembering threats it's encountered and then mounting stronger defenses in the future. Now, a new study unpacks how cells keep one type of immune memory from fading, and the findings might matter for treating diseases like cancer and Alzheimer's disease. The research zoomed in on immune cells' epigenetics ‪—‬ the methods that cells use to control genes without changing their underlying DNA codes. This can involve changing how DNA is packaged inside cells, for example. DNA molecules are typically wound around tiny spools inside cells, and their gene activity depends on how tightly or loosely they're wound. Molecules called epigenetic markers can grab hold of the spool to tweak how the DNA is wound and thus activate or silence certain genes. Past research found epigenetic changes can prime immune cells against threats. The immune system's first line of defense — innate immune cells — can be switched into an activated state so they're ready to go if they encounter a germ. This form of immune memory, known as "trained immunity," broadly enhances the cells' defenses, enabling them to respond to threats more quickly and powerfully than "untrained" …

title: Rare swarm of asteroids from the solar system’s youth found trailing Neptune around the sun
summary: Astronomers have found two rare asteroids trailing Neptune in Vera C. Rubin Observatory data. The rocks, called Neptune's L5 Trojans, could illuminate the conditions of the infant solar system.
body: Astronomers using the Vera C. Rubin Observatory have discovered two ancient Trojan asteroids trailing Neptune ‪—‬ the first new ones to be spotted in 15 years. The findings, published Oct. 15 in The Astrophysical Journal Letters , could improve our understanding of the early solar system while reinforcing the Rubin Observatory's potential to unearth new cosmic objects during its brisk scans of the sky. Trojan asteroids are icy, rocky bodies that dwell in a planet's vicinity but don't orbit it. Instead, these asteroids orbit the sun, following the same path as the planet. Trojan asteroids exist in distinct swarms roughly 60 degrees ahead of and behind the planet. At these points, called Lagrange points 4 and 5 (L4 and L5), respectively, the gravitational tugs of the sun and the planet balance each other, essentially "locking" the asteroids in position, according to NASA . However, very few Trojans actually hang around for billions of years. Such asteroids are likely planetary building block remnants from the solar system's infancy, and detecting them in the outer solar system can be challenging.
